steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a continual learning paper that proposes a class-prototype conditional diffusion model with gradient projection for generative replay. Motivate it with catastrophic forgetting and the weaknesses of existing generative replay methods, describe the idea, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Continual learning and catastrophic forgetting
- Generative replay: generator plus classifier
- From GAN/VAE replay to diffusion-based DDGR, and its weakness
- Our method: GPPDM (class prototypes + gradient projection)
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Continual learning
- networks acquire and accumulate knowledge from sequentially arriving tasks
- mimics human learning; models that adapt quickly to evolving real-world environments
- main challenge: Catastrophic Forgetting (CF) - learn new tasks without losing old knowledge, esp. without access to old data

## Generative replay (GR)
- CL strategies: preserve knowledge from previous tasks
- crucial when privacy prevents keeping old raw data and task ID unknown at test time
- generative models / GR effective: learn distribution of past data
- two parts: generator (samples from prior tasks) + classifier (trained on them)
- classifier handles current-task samples and generated samples -> mitigates CF

## GAN/VAE -> DDGR
- early GR: GAN and Variational Auto Encoder (VAE); single direction (generator to classifier); recycle generated samples -> image quality declines
- DDGR: Diffusion Models (DMs), bi-directional generator/classifier interaction
- generator-to-classifier: denoise noisy images with class info from previous tasks -> high-quality samples to train classifier
- classifier-to-generator: classifier pretrained on previous tasks guides generator
- our experiments: generated image quality drops over a lengthy sequence of tasks -> hurts retention

## GPPDM
- Gradient Projection Class-Prototype conditional Diffusion Model
- classifier helps DM learn additional suitable prototypes -> preserve abstract info of old data, reduce DDGR's gradual forgetting
- replay generation uses labels + learned prototypes -> better image quality
- after training class y: label and prototype (DM inputs) become invariant
- want old-task representations in current task close to original ones -> matches GPM strategy
- inject GPM into DM, specifically Cross-Attention layers; streamlined and effective

## Contributions
- training DM by learning class prototypes (most representative examples of previous classes); class-prototype conditional denoising -> high-quality images
- novel GPM design for DM; works in harmony with prototypes; simple implementation
- benchmark results: significantly outperforms state of the art; higher average accuracy, lower average forgetting rate

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Continual Learning (CL) is when neural networks progressively acquire and accumulate knowledge from tasks that arrive sequentially over time. CL mimics how humans learn, and it aims to build models that can adapt quickly to real-world environments that keep evolving. The main challenge in CL is Catastrophic Forgetting (CF): the model needs to learn new tasks without losing the knowledge it acquired before, especially when the old data can't be accessed.

Continual learning strategies mostly focus on overcoming CF by preserving knowledge from previous tasks. This matters especially when privacy concerns mean the old raw data cannot be kept and the task ID is unknown during testing. In these cases, methods that use generative models, specifically Generative Replay (GR), are notably effective because they learn the distribution of the past data. GR approaches usually use a two-part system made of a generator and a classifier. The generator generates samples from prior tasks and these are used to train the classifier. The classifier should classify samples from the current task but also categorize the generated samples well, and this helps to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.

- early GR used GAN and Variational Auto Encoder (VAE): one direction (generator to classifier), recycle generated samples -> image quality declines
- DDGR uses Diffusion Models (DMs), bi-directional: generator denoises noisy images with class info to train classifier; pretrained classifier guides generator
- our experiments: quality drops over a long sequence of tasks -> forgetting
- GPPDM (Gradient Projection Class-Prototype conditional Diffusion Model): classifier helps DM learn prototypes that keep abstract info of old data; replay uses labels + prototypes
- label and prototype of a trained class y become invariant -> keep old representations close -> GPM, injected into DM Cross-Attention layers
- contributions: class-prototype learning for DM; GPM design for DM; benchmark results beat state of the art (higher average accuracy, lower average forgetting rate)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Continual Learning (CL) is when neural networks progressively acquire and accumulate knowledge from tasks that arrive sequentially over time. CL mimics how humans learn, and it aims to build models that can adapt quickly to real-world environments that keep evolving. The main challenge in CL is Catastrophic Forgetting (CF): the model needs to learn new tasks without losing the knowledge it acquired before, especially when the old data can't be accessed.

Continual learning strategies mostly focus on overcoming CF by preserving knowledge from previous tasks. This matters especially when privacy concerns mean the old raw data cannot be kept and the task ID is unknown during testing. In these cases, methods that use generative models, specifically Generative Replay (GR), are notably effective because they learn the distribution of the past data. GR approaches usually use a two-part system made of a generator and a classifier. The generator generates samples from prior tasks and these are used to train the classifier. The classifier should classify samples from the current task but also categorize the generated samples well, and this helps to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.

For GR approaches, the first efforts used GAN and Variational Auto Encoder (VAE) architectures. These work in one direction only (from generator to classifier) and they recycle generated samples, so the image quality gradually goes down. The recent DDGR method uses Diffusion Models (DMs) to prevent forgetting in generative models more effectively. DDGR has a bi-directional interaction between the generator and the classifier. In the generator-to-classifier direction, the generator makes high-quality samples by denoising noisy images with class information from previous tasks, and these samples are used to train the classifier. In the other direction, classifier-to-generator, the classifier that was pretrained on previous tasks guides the generator to synthesize high-quality samples from these tasks. But in our experimental studies we saw a noticeable decrease in the quality of the generated images when the model was trained on a long sequence of tasks, and this hurts its capacity to retain the knowledge from earlier tasks.

In this paper we introduce the Gradient Projection Class-Prototype conditional Diffusion Model (GPPDM) to address catastrophic forgetting in Continual Learning more efficiently. Given the bi-directional relationship in GR strategies described above, in our model the classifier helps the diffusion model learn additional suitable prototypes. The prototypes help preserve abstract information about old data, which reduces DDGR's disadvantage of gradually forgetting old knowledge. So when the diffusion model generates replay data in new tasks to train the classifier, it uses information from both the labels and the learned prototypes, and the generated images have better quality. Also, after a class y is trained, this label and its prototype, which are inputs of the DM, become invariant components. So to exploit the learned prototypes more efficiently and limit CF further, we want to preserve the corresponding knowledge on the DM more effectively, so that the representations of old task data in the current task stay as close as possible to their representations when they first arrived. This desideratum matches the strategy of GPM, and it inspires us to design a new approach that injects GPM into the DM, specifically into the Cross-Attention layers. This approach is streamlined and also effective at avoiding forgetting. Our main contributions are:

- We propose an efficient training technique for the diffusion model that learns class prototypes, which capture the most representative examples of classes from previous tasks. This makes it possible to generate high-quality images through class-prototype conditional denoising.

- We suggest a new design of GPM for DM to reduce forgetting further. Together with the learned class prototypes it works in harmony to preserve old knowledge effectively, and the implementation is simple.

- Results on benchmark datasets show that our method significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art model, with higher average accuracy and lower average forgetting rate.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Continual Learning (CL) is a process in which neural networks progressively acquire and accumulate knowledge from tasks arriving sequentially over time. Mimicking human learning, CL aims to develop models that can swiftly adapt to evolving real-world environments. The primary challenge in CL is Catastrophic Forgetting (CF) [1]: the model needs to learn new tasks without losing previously acquired knowledge, particularly when old data can no longer be accessed.

Continual learning strategies primarily focus on overcoming CF by preserving knowledge from previous tasks. This is particularly crucial when privacy concerns prevent the retention of old raw data and the task ID remains unknown during testing. In such cases, methods that employ generative models, specifically Generative Replay (GR), are notably effective for learning the distribution of past data. GR approaches [2,3,4] usually adopt a two-part system consisting of a generator and a classifier. The generator produces samples from prior tasks, which are then used to train the classifier. The classifier must not only classify samples from the current task but also correctly categorize the generated samples, which helps to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.

Initial GR efforts utilized GAN and Variational Auto Encoder (VAE) architectures, which operate in a single direction (from generator to classifier) and recycle generated samples, leading to a gradual decline in image quality. The recent DDGR method [4] leverages Diffusion Models (DMs) to prevent forgetting in generative models more effectively. DDGR employs a bi-directional interaction between the generator and the classifier. In the generator-to-classifier direction, the generator creates high-quality samples by denoising noisy images with class information from previous tasks, and these samples are used to train the classifier. In the classifier-to-generator direction, the classifier pretrained on previous tasks guides the generator in synthesizing high-quality samples from these tasks. However, our experimental studies revealed a noticeable decrease in the quality of generated images when the model was trained on a lengthy sequence of tasks, which weakens its capacity to retain knowledge from earlier tasks.

To address catastrophic forgetting in Continual Learning more efficiently, this paper introduces the Gradient Projection Class-Prototype conditional Diffusion Model (GPPDM). Building on the bi-directional relationship of GR strategies described above, in our model the classifier helps the diffusion model learn additional suitable prototypes. These prototypes help preserve abstract information about old data, reducing DDGR's tendency to gradually forget old knowledge. Consequently, when generating replay data in new tasks for training the classifier, the diffusion model uses the information from both the labels and the corresponding learned prototypes to obtain generated images of better quality. Moreover, after a class y has been trained, this label and its prototype, which are inputs of the DM, become invariant components. Therefore, to exploit the learned prototypes more efficiently and further limit CF, we wish to preserve the corresponding knowledge on the DM more effectively, keeping the representations of old task data in the current task as close as possible to their representations when they first arrived. This desideratum aligns with the strategy of GPM [5], which inspires us to design a novel approach that injects GPM into the DM, specifically into its Cross-Attention layers. This approach is streamlined and also effective in avoiding forgetting. In summary, our primary contributions are as follows:

- We propose an efficient training technique for the diffusion model that learns class prototypes, which capture the most representative examples of classes from previous tasks. This facilitates the generation of high-quality images through class-prototype conditional denoising.

- To further reduce forgetting, we suggest a novel design of GPM for DM. Combined with the learned class prototypes, it works in harmony to preserve old knowledge effectively, with a simple implementation.

- Comprehensive results on benchmark datasets show that our proposed method significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art model, achieving higher average accuracy and a lower average forgetting rate.

References:
[1] French, R.M.: Catastrophic forgetting in connectionist networks. Trends in cognitive sciences 3 (4), 128–135 (1999)
[2] Shin, H., Lee, J.K., Kim, J., Kim, J.: Continual learning with deep generative replay. In: Guyon, I., Luxburg, U.V., Bengio, S., Wallach, H., Fergus, R., Vishwanathan, S., Garnett, R. (eds.) Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. vol. 30. Curran Associates, Inc. (2017)
[3] Kemker, R., Kanan, C.: Fearnet: Brain-inspired model for incremental learning. In: International Conference on Learning Representations (2018), https://openreview.net/forum?id=SJ1Xmf-Rb
[4] Gao, R., Liu, W.: DDGR: Continual learning with deep diffusion-based generative replay. In: Krause, A., Brunskill, E., Cho, K., Engelhardt, B., Sabato, S., Scarlett, J. (eds.) Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, vol. 202, pp. 10744–10763 (23–29 Jul 2023)
[5] Saha, G., Garg, I., Roy, K.: Gradient projection memory for continual learning. In: International Conference on Learning Representations (2021), https://openreview.net/forum?id=3AOj0RCNC2
